sources.name: BleepingComputer

sources.name: SecurityWeek
sources.title: 1Password Breach Exposes Customer Data, Internal Source Code

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: 1Password Hacked, Customer Data and Source Code Stolen in GitHub Account Breach

incidents.title: 1Password: compromised employee GitHub account used to push malicious code and steal data
incidents.tldrRootCause: An employee's corporate GitHub account was taken over, likely via a stolen credential or token, and used to deploy malicious code.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The reporting says the attacker used the compromised account to push malicious code to backend services, then stole customer records and internal source code. How the account was taken over is not stated, so the credential theft is an inference; 1Password says vaults were not accessed.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, the technique applies to any GitHub organisation where one developer account can push code that deploys to production without a second approval.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: If one of your GitHub accounts or tokens is taken over, and a single account can merge and deploy, an attacker can ship malicious code into your cloud backend the same way.
lockItDown: In GitHub rulesets or branch protection for branches that deploy to production, confirm pull request approval by another person is required and that admins cannot bypass it.
In GitHub Environments for production deployments, confirm required reviewers are set, and review the organisation audit log for newly added personal access tokens, SSH keys and OAuth apps.
incidents.roleAngle: One developer account led to both source code and customer data, which makes the case for two-person control on every path from GitHub to production.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: Remus malware steals Gmail messages via fake Google Sheets extension

incidents.title: Remus infostealer reads Gmail through a fake Google Sheets Chrome extension
incidents.evidenceQuote: stealing Gmail messages through a stealthy malicious Chrome extension
incidents.tldrRootCause: An infostealer installs a malicious Chrome extension posing as Google Sheets, which then reads Gmail messages from the logged-in browser.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The Remus infostealer uses a malicious Chrome extension to read Gmail from inside the browser session. Its operators marketed this as a Gmail zero-day, but the evidence describes an extension, not a flaw in Gmail; how Remus first lands on the machine is not stated.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, if an infostealer runs on a laptop where Chrome is signed in to Gmail; look for a Google Sheets extension nobody installed.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: An infected Mac or Windows laptop gets a rogue extension added to Chrome, which reads mail (including password resets and cloud alerts) from the active session.
lockItDown: Open chrome://extensions on your laptops and remove anything you did not install, especially an extension named like Google Sheets that did not come from your own install.
If you manage Chrome centrally, check in the admin console's extension policy that installs are limited to an allowlist rather than open to any extension.
incidents.roleAngle: Session-level theft via an extension sidesteps MFA, so extension allowlisting is an identity control as much as an endpoint one.

sources.name: The Record (Recorded Future)
sources.title: Software giant SAP confirms cyber incident amid reports of source code breach

sources.name: SecurityWeek
sources.title: SAP Confirms Cyberattack, Source Code Reportedly Compromised

incidents.title: SAP confirms incident; stolen employee GitHub tokens reportedly used to copy and alter code
incidents.evidenceQuote: hackers reportedly used stolen employee tokens to copy and alter source code
incidents.tldrRootCause: Attackers reportedly used stolen employee tokens to access SAP's GitHub and copy and alter source code.
incidents.realisticRootCause: SAP confirmed an incident and detected suspicious activity on GitHub; reporting says stolen employee tokens were used to copy and alter source code. How the tokens were stolen is not stated in the evidence.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, the technique applies to any GitHub organisation: a long-lived employee token with repo write access is enough.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A personal access token or OAuth token lifted from a developer laptop or a CI secret would let an attacker clone and push to your repositories without touching SSO.
lockItDown: In GitHub, go to Settings > Developer settings > Personal access tokens and revoke tokens that are unused, have no expiry or have broad repo scope; at org level, review the personal access token policy and consider restr
Check the organisation audit log for unusual clone or push activity by token, and confirm branch protection requires review on default branches.
incidents.roleAngle: Tokens are bearer credentials that bypass SSO and MFA, so token lifetime and scope are the controls that matter here.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: SYS010 malware abuses browser management to spy on Gmail, Outlook

incidents.title: SYS01 infostealer enrols browsers in management to force a mail-stealing extension
incidents.evidenceQuote: SYS01 infostealer malware delivered through Meta ads is enrolling browsers into enterprise-style management
incidents.tldrRootCause: Users are lured by Meta ads into running the SYS01 infostealer, which enrols the browser in management and force-installs an extension.
incidents.realisticRootCause: A new SYS01 version sets enterprise-style browser management on the victim's machine so it can force-install an extension. That extension steals sensitive data, including Gmail and Outlook emails.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, if someone on a Mac or Windows laptop runs a download from a malicious Meta ad; unmanaged personal browsers are the most exposed.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A lure from an ad leads to malware on a laptop, which then controls the browser by policy and reads webmail sessions, including any used for work.
lockItDown: Open chrome://management (or edge://management) and confirm the browser is managed only by your own organization, or not at all on personal devices.
Open chrome://policy and look for force-installed extension entries (ExtensionInstallForcelist) you do not recognise.
incidents.roleAngle: Browser policy is now a persistence mechanism; unexpected 'managed by your organization' banners on unmanaged devices are a detection signal.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Hackers Trojanize Official Q-Dir and DesktopOK Downloads to Deliver Remote Access Malware

incidents.title: Official Q-Dir and DesktopOK downloads and updates trojanized with remote access malware
incidents.evidenceQuote: tampered with Q-Dir and DesktopOK installation files distributed via the official SoftwareOK website
incidents.attackSurface: Windows utilities / vendor download and update channel
incidents.tldrRootCause: Attackers tampered with Q-Dir and DesktopOK installers served from the official SoftwareOK site, including through the update process.
incidents.realisticRootCause: Researchers describe a software supply chain attack in which malicious files were served both from the official download page and during updates of already installed copies. How the SoftwareOK site or its update channel was compromised is not stated in the excerpt.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, if any Windows laptop you use or manage has Q-Dir or DesktopOK installed or recently updated.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A Windows laptop that installed or auto-updated either tool could now be running remote access malware, putting cloud, GitHub and SSO sessions on that machine at risk.
lockItDown: Check Windows Settings > Apps > Installed apps, or your endpoint software inventory, for Q-Dir and DesktopOK on Windows laptops.
If either is present, treat the machine as potentially compromised until checked against the researchers' published indicators, and re-issue credentials and sessions used on it.
incidents.roleAngle: Small freeware utilities with their own update channels are a supply chain path that bypasses most package and code review controls.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: North Korea-Linked PolinRider Poisons Over 7,600 GitHub Repositories to Spread Malware

incidents.title: PolinRider campaign compromises over 7,600 GitHub repositories owned by real developers
incidents.tldrRootCause: Not disclosed: how the developers' accounts or repos were taken over is not in the excerpt, only that real repos were poisoned with a Python loader.
incidents.realisticRootCause: Not disclosed in the evidence. Apiiro reports that over 7,600 repositories were compromised, most belonging to real developers rather than throwaway accounts. Some had a Python loader planted that fetches next-stage payloads, and the activity may date back to February 2025.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Possibly: your own GitHub repos could be poisoned the same way, or you could clone and run code from a repo that already has been.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: Either a compromised developer account pushes a loader into a repo you own, or you or your CI pull and run code from one of the poisoned repos.
lockItDown: Review your GitHub security log, plus personal access tokens, SSH keys and authorized OAuth apps in account settings, for anything you do not recognise.
Check recent commit history on your repos and on third-party repos you build from for unexpected commits adding or changing Python files.
incidents.roleAngle: A repo owned by a legitimate, long-standing developer account is not evidence that its latest commit is trustworthy.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: Fake paid expert interviews impersonate brands to steal Google logins

incidents.title: "GoodGuys" phishing uses fake paid expert interviews to steal Google and Okta logins
incidents.evidenceQuote: steal corporate Google and Okta credentials using fake invitations to paid expert interviews and webinars
incidents.tldrRootCause: Fake invitations to paid expert interviews and webinars, impersonating major brands, lead staff to hand over corporate Google and Okta credentials.
incidents.realisticRootCause: An ongoing campaign impersonates brands including Google, Nvidia, Accenture and SpaceX and uses interview and webinar invitations as the lure. The teaser does not say how the credentials are captured or whether MFA is bypassed.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes. Security and cloud staff are plausible targets for paid expert interview lures, and the campaign goes after corporate Google and Okta logins.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: An invitation reaches you or a colleague, the sign-in step captures SSO credentials, and those credentials open cloud consoles and GitHub behind SSO.
lockItDown: In the Okta authentication policies or Google Workspace 2-Step Verification settings, confirm that admin and cloud-console access requires a phishing-resistant method (FIDO2 security key or passkey), not push or OTP.
Review Okta System Log or Google Workspace login audit events for sign-ins from new devices or unfamiliar locations, especially for users who recently received interview or webinar invitations.
incidents.roleAngle: A good example for awareness briefings: the lure flatters professional expertise rather than using the usual invoice or password-reset themes.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: New NFS2ROOT Linux flaw can let attackers gain root privileges

incidents.title: NFS2ROOT: 12-year-old Linux kernel NFS server flaw allows remote root (CVE-2026-99362)
incidents.evidenceQuote: allows remote attackers to gain root privileges
incidents.attackSurface: Linux kernel NFS server on cloud hosts and nodes
incidents.tldrRootCause: A critical flaw in the Linux kernel's NFS server lets a remote attacker gain root; the evidence does not report exploitation in the wild.
incidents.realisticRootCause: CVE-2026-99362 is in the kernel's Network File System server and has been present for about 12 years. The teaser gives no affected versions, required configuration or patch status.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Possibly: look for Linux VMs or Kubernetes nodes that run the kernel NFS server (nfsd) and are reachable on the NFS port.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A self-managed Linux host exporting NFS in your cloud accounts, reachable by an attacker over the network, could be taken over as root and used to pivot into workloads and their credentials.
lockItDown: Review security groups and firewall rules in AWS, GCP and Azure for inbound TCP 2049 (NFS) allowed from wide ranges, and restrict it to known clients.
Inventory Linux VMs and Kubernetes nodes that run the kernel NFS server, and schedule the distribution's kernel update for them once it is available.
incidents.roleAngle: Self-managed NFS exports on cloud VMs are often forgotten; this is a reason to find them.

sources.name: Microsoft Security Blog (Threat Intelligence)
sources.title: What defenders need to know about ARTEX, the agentic AI framework threat actors abuse

incidents.title: Microsoft: ARTEX AI pentest framework abused by state and criminal actors to automate attacks
incidents.tldrRootCause: Not a single incident; threat actors use the public ARTEX framework to automate reconnaissance, credential attacks and web exploitation.
incidents.realisticRootCause: Microsoft reports that multiple state-sponsored and financially motivated groups have integrated ARTEX into their tooling since its July 2026 release. Recent campaigns used it to search public repositories for exposed secrets, enable supply chain compromise and scan internet-facing systems.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, if secrets are committed to your public GitHub repositories or you have unpatched internet-facing services; this tooling finds both faster.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: An automated agent searching public repositories could find a cloud key or token committed to your GitHub organisation and use it against your cloud accounts.
lockItDown: In GitHub organisation settings, confirm secret scanning and push protection are enabled for all repositories, and review any open secret scanning alerts.
Review Microsoft's post for the ARTEX network and system activity indicators and hunting queries, and check them against your logs.
incidents.roleAngle: Automation shortens the time between a secret being exposed in a public repository and it being used.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Microsoft Store App Found Delivering Vinci RAT Capable of Remote System Control

incidents.title: Fake snipping-tool site leads to Microsoft Store app that delivers Vinci RAT
incidents.evidenceQuote: begins with a redirection to a bogus site for a sniping tool
incidents.tldrRootCause: Users are redirected to a fake snipping-tool site that serves a Microsoft-signed installer, and a Microsoft Store app delivers the Vinci RAT.
incidents.realisticRootCause: eSentire reports that the chain starts at snipp.codes-team[.]com, which serves a Microsoft-signed "Snipping-Tool.exe". The teaser is cut off, so the steps between the installer and the RAT are not in the evidence.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes, on Windows laptops where users can install Store apps or run downloaded installers, since a Microsoft signature makes the file look trustworthy.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: Someone on a Windows laptop searching for a screenshot tool lands on the fake site and installs the app, giving the attacker remote control of a machine that holds cloud and GitHub sessions.
lockItDown: Check Intune or Group Policy to see whether Microsoft Store installs on managed Windows devices are restricted to an approved list.
Search EDR and DNS logs for the domain snipp.codes-team[.]com and for executions of a file named Snipping-Tool.exe from user download folders.
incidents.roleAngle: A Microsoft signature or Store listing is not proof an app is safe; allowlisting by publisher alone would not have stopped this.

sources.name: The Hacker News
sources.title: Most Wanted: The Phishing Kits and Techniques Getting Past Security Controls

incidents.title: Vendor research: phishing kits ranked by how often they get past email and web filtering
incidents.evidenceQuote: we measure this as breakthrough rate: The share of attacks that get past email security, web gateways, and safe browsing to reach the user
incidents.tldrRootCause: No specific compromise; Push Security research on phishing kits that get past email security, web gateways and safe browsing.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The piece measures how often phishing kits reach the user despite filtering controls. The excerpt does not name the kits or the evasion techniques.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Yes in principle: any SSO login reachable from a browser is a phishing target, and this research says filtering alone often does not stop the page arriving.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: A phishing page that gets past mail and web filtering reaches your browser and captures an SSO session, which then opens cloud consoles and GitHub.
lockItDown: In your identity provider's authentication or conditional access policy, confirm admin and cloud-console roles require a phishing-resistant method (passkey or FIDO2 key), with no fallback to push or OTP.
Review the IdP sign-in log for recent successful logins from unfamiliar devices or locations on privileged accounts.
incidents.roleAngle: Useful evidence that filtering is not a sufficient phishing control and that authentication strength is the control that holds.

incidents.tldrRootCause: A publicly disclosed, unpatched Cacti flaw lets an unauthenticated HTTP session reach command execution; no attacks are reported yet.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The proof of concept, tracked as 4HTTP2SHELL and 4HTTP2ROOT, reportedly reaches command execution in four HTTP requests via guest access. It has no CVE identifier, and the evidence does not report exploitation in the wild.

incidents.howItCouldHitYou: Cacti is not in your stated footprint, so there is no direct path unless an operations team hosts it on infrastructure you cover.

incidents.tldrRootCause: Remote attackers exploit CVE-2026-103406 in Juniper Session Smart Conductor to run arbitrary commands as root.

sources.title: File under "Will is not surprised": Security product vendor Checkpoint compromised by use of JavaScript math.random() fu

incidents.title: Check Point reportedly compromised through insecure use of JavaScript Math.random()
incidents.evidenceQuote: compromised by use of JavaScript math.random() function in something that could benefit from being cryptographically secure
incidents.tldrRootCause: A single social post says predictable Math.random() output was used where cryptographically secure randomness was needed.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The post attributes the compromise to a non-cryptographic random number generator used for a security-sensitive value. It does not say which product or component was affected or what was accessed, and whether the flaw was internet-facing is an assumption.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Only if you run Check Point products; the evidence does not say which one, so wait for the vendor advisory.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: Check Point is not in the stated footprint; the path would run through an affected Check Point product, which the post does not identify.
incidents.roleAngle: Tokens, session IDs and reset codes generated with Math.random() are predictable; this is a common code-review finding.

sources.name: SecurityWeek
sources.title: Hex Package Manager Warns of Potential Data Breach

incidents.title: Hex.pm package registry flaw allowed command execution on its web servers
incidents.evidenceQuote: A vulnerability in hex.pm allowed hackers to run commands on web servers.
incidents.tldrRootCause: A vulnerability in hex.pm let attackers run commands on the registry's web servers; the specific flaw is not described.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The evidence says a hex.pm vulnerability allowed command execution on its web servers. No data modification was found, but database reads are not logged, so data access cannot be ruled out.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Only if your teams publish or pull Elixir/Erlang packages from hex.pm; look for mix.exs or rebar.config files and Hex API keys in CI secrets.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: Hex is not in your stated footprint; the path would be Hex account data or API keys being read from the registry database if your organisation has Hex accounts.
incidents.roleAngle: A registry that cannot rule out data theft because reads are not logged is a useful example when arguing for read-access logging on your own data stores.

sources.name: SecurityWeek
sources.title: 100,000 Potentially Impacted by Colorado Data Breach

incidents.title: myColorado digital ID app breached; up to 100,000 users' uploaded data accessed
incidents.attackSurface: Government digital ID / document storage app
incidents.tldrRootCause: Not disclosed. Attackers breached the myColorado app and accessed user-uploaded data; the method is not given.
incidents.realisticRootCause: Not disclosed. The evidence says only that hackers breached the digital identification and document storage application and accessed user-uploaded data.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Not through your work footprint; it affects people who uploaded documents to the myColorado app.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: There is no path to the reader's environment; this is a state government application breach with no stated cause.
incidents.roleAngle: Another example of identity-document stores as high-value targets.

sources.name: GitHub Critical Advisories
sources.title: GHSA Critical (composer:tastyigniter/tastyigniter): TastyIgniter allows Remote Code Execution (RCE) via Unrestricted file upload in Media Manager

incidents.title: TastyIgniter: admin media manager accepts .htaccess upload, allowing RCE (CVE-2026-69179)
incidents.evidenceQuote: Media manager accepts `.htaccess` file which can be used to perform RCE.
incidents.tldrRootCause: A logged-in admin can upload a .htaccess file through the Media Manager and use it to make uploaded files run as PHP.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The upload filter does not block .htaccess, so an authenticated admin can change the handler for the upload directory and run PHP. The advisory's proof of concept requires an admin login, and no exploitation in the wild is reported.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Not through the stated footprint; this only matters if you host a TastyIgniter site.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: There is no path to this reader unless a TastyIgniter instance runs in an environment they manage, and even then the attacker needs admin credentials first.

sources.name: GitHub Critical Advisories
sources.title: GHSA Critical (composer:tastyigniter/tastyigniter): TastyIgniter mail template editor allows remote code execution via server-side template injection

incidents.title: TastyIgniter mail template editor allows admin-level RCE via template injection (CVE-2026-69178)
incidents.evidenceQuote: The Mail templates is vulnerable to SSTI and did not perform an validation and sanitization
incidents.tldrRootCause: An admin with mail template permission can inject PHP into a template and have the server execute it.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The mail template body is not validated or sanitised, so server-side template injection gives arbitrary PHP execution when the template is tested. It requires an authenticated admin with the Admin.MailTemplates permission; the advisory reports no exploitation.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: Only if you host TastyIgniter, a restaurant ordering platform; look for the composer package tastyigniter/tastyigniter.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: There is no path unless a TastyIgniter instance exists in your estate, and even then the attacker needs an admin account first.

incidents.title: Roundup: the biggest data breach class action settlements of 2026
incidents.tldrRootCause: Not an incident: a legal roundup of class action settlements for breaches from past years.
incidents.realisticRootCause: The piece summarises settlement agreements announced in 2026 for earlier breaches. It describes no new compromise or vulnerability.
incidents.couldThisHappenToMe: No; this is a legal summary, not a threat.
incidents.howItCouldHitYou: There is no technical path; it is only relevant as background on breach litigation costs.
incidents.roleAngle: Settlement figures can support business cases for security spend.
